caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Gabon's debt tracks oil with a ratchet effect: it falls in booms and jumps in busts, never fully returning. From 20.1% of GDP in 2008 it rose after the 2014 oil crash to 63.9% by 2016, then COVID and a second oil shock drove it to 83.0% in 2020, the series high. The 2021-22 oil rebound brought only partial relief (66.4% in 2022), and renewed borrowing plus weaker oil pushed it back to a projected 78.6% in 2025. Gabon has issued Eurobonds and borrowed from China; IMF programs have pressed for consolidation with limited success. The structural problem is a public wage bill and spending level built for $100 oil in a $70-80 world.
inflation_management: Gabon's inflation has been low throughout, anchored by the Central African CFA franc's peg to the euro: it peaked at 5.3% in 2008 and troughed at -1.4% in 2006, averaging around 2%. Even the 2022 global shock produced only 4.3%, easing to a projected 2.0% in 2025. The BEAC's regional monetary policy has delivered exemplary price stability through coups, oil crashes, and pandemics. But as in other CEMAC oil states, the peg's stability conceals a competitiveness problem: with oil in long-term decline as a share of output, the real exchange rate offers no cushion for diversification, and adjustment falls entirely on fiscal policy.

key_events.event: Omar Bongo died after 42 years in power; son Ali Bongo succeeded him.
Oil price crash ended the boom; debt began its climb from 34.3% of GDP.
Disputed re-election of Ali Bongo triggered violent protests; a 2019 coup attempt failed.
COVID-19 and oil crash pushed debt to 83.0% of GDP, the series high.
August 30, 2023: military ousted Ali Bongo after a disputed election, ending 56 years of Bongo rule; General Brice Oligui Nguema took power.
April 12, 2025: Oligui won the presidential election with about 90% of the vote, formalizing the transition.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued oil dependence with debt near 80% of GDP and low inflation under the CFA peg. Upside depends on whether the new government diversifies (manganese, timber processing) and controls the wage bill; downside is another oil downturn forcing abrupt adjustment. Uncertainty is moderate: the 2023-25 transition was orderly by regional standards, but the economic model is unchanged and oil output is mature.
